radicals.meaningMnemonic: This <radical>box</radical> is open. There could be any number of things inside, but for now all you need to know is the meaning of this radical, which is box.

A (modified) prison radical containing a person radical. What does a person experience in prison? <radical>Lack</radical>. Prison is all about lack — lack of freedom, lack of the comforts of home, lack of privacy, lack of conversation. Yep, the life of a person in prison is defined by lack.

This is the <radical>stamp</radical> radical — the inking kind, not the postage kind. Why? Because it looks like a stamp stick! The top parts are thicker on one side so you can get a good grip. It even looks like the letter P — which just happens to be the last letter in "stamp"!

The radicals ground and big make up this radical. There's a big guy on the ground... who is that big guy? Embarrassingly, it's your <radical>husband</radical>. Feel the shame that he got knocked down on the ground. By what? Who? How? (It doesn't matter.)

Don't confuse this with 未 (jet), though. See how 未 has a little tail at the end? That's because jets and other planes have tails, while husbands don't. At least I'd sure hope yours doesn't.

Under a cliff, you spot a cross, slightly tilted. The cross is there to mark a famous <radical>clan</radical> that once ruled the lands below the cliff. It's a pretty unique cross, so whenever you see it there under the cliff, you'll know it honors the clan who lived there.
This looks like a <radical>boat</radical> coming toward you in the water. See the sail billowing on top and the reflection on the water? Yep, that's a boat. The boatiest boat that ever boated.
This is a <radical>fish</radical>. Kind of a funny-looking fish, with a weird head on top, a squat scaly body, and a tail fanning out underneath it. See the fish? Yeah, you see it.
See the cool wing on the bottom? See the head with the neat feather coming out of the top? This is a <radical>bird</radical>. Tweet tweet!

Flowers that grow out of the ground of a rice paddy after you bury fins there will grow <radical>yellow</radical>. Why? Because yellow is the color of a fish's soul, so planting flowers over their fins will turn them into a nice, pretty yellow.
If you boil a village, everything will turn <radical>black</radical>. Just imagine all those roads melting and coating everything in black tar. Picture it! It looks like Pompeii. (Oof, too soon?)

You take your head and pack clay dirt around it to just above your mouth. You need the <radical>circumference</radical> of your head for your helmet maker, and sending them a clay dirt mold of your head will just do the trick. That way they'll know your head's exact circumference!
See the <radical>wing</radical>? It's kind of like a bat wing with webbing. Either way, it's just a wing.
What happens when you put a flat surface on top of a pair of legs? You get a <radical>table</radical>.

This radical looks kind of like a <radical>temple</radical>, don't you think? With all the layers and stuff? Just picture the top part as a roof, and the drop-looking bit at the bottom as a giant temple bell, with a monk standing beside it and ringing it with a large wooden beam. You see this kinda thing every day at a temple.

This radical already looks like a <radical>gate</radical>, right? A high gate with pillars on either side and two small gate doors, way up at the top for some reason. Worst gate ever in terms of security, but definitely still a gate.
This kinda looks like a head with an arm under it pointing up at itself. That's why this radical means <radical>oneself</radical>. One points to oneself when one wants to… indicate oneself…

This is the radical for <radical>south</radical>. See how it's pointing south? You can think of the cross on top as a compass rose, and the arrow below (that ¥-looking part) as pointing down south. It's a compass pointing nowhere but south!

Who's in the coffin next to that child? It's his <radical>teacher</radical>. Teachers are pretty much dead around 3 p.m. every day, and it's the kids in their class who wear them down. It ain't easy being a teacher, you know.
This radical looks just like a top hat. That's why it's <radical>top hat</radical>!

This is an <radical>elephant</radical> — or at least, a wannabe elephant. Look closely. It's actually a family of pigs, and the mama is wearing an elephant mask on her head for some reason. See the big ears and trunk on top? She wants to be an elephant so badly that she dressed up like one.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You go down a <radical>street</radical> that cuts through a <radical>rice paddy</radical> and leads to a <radical>box</radical>. When you open the box at the end of the street, you see it's full of <kanji>image</kanji>s. Image after image. <kanji>Drawing</kanji>, <kanji>painting</kanji>, you name it. Someone must have left this box of images here.
kanji.meaningHint: What are the images of, anyway? Well, it's better not to say out loud. Just think of the kind of image you enjoy looking at most. That's what's in the box at the end of the street. Aren't you the lucky one?
kanji.readingMnemonic: Okay, I didn't want to tell you this, but the <kanji>image</kanji>s are all <kanji>drawing</kanji>s and <kanji>painting</kanji>s of <reading>ga</reading>rgoyles (が) and <reading>cock</reading>s (かく). Male chickens, that is. Turns out that's what you wanted to see most. Don't worry, no one is judging you.
kanji.readingHint: Try to see the images of the gargoyles. Winged, stony monsters. Very cool. And the roosters? Colorful little dinosaurs. What's not to like?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You've seen this as a radical before, and the kanji means the same thing — <kanji>south</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: If you keep up with your radicals, your kanji studies will never go south. Haha! Go south! Get it? I said g—
kanji.readingMnemonic: Think about the <kanji>south</kanji>. What's down there? <reading>Mean Amy</reading> (みなみ) lives down there. Think of the last mean thing she did to you and imagine it while yelling out "MEAN AMYYYYY" at the sky.
kanji.readingHint: Picture Mean Amy down in the south, saying mean things in her American southern accent: "Y'all don't come back now, ya hear?" Man, Mean Amy is so mean. And southern.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical it comes from. <radical>Lack</radical> becomes <kanji>Lack</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: If you know the radical you know this.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
To remember けつ, we use the word "ketsup." It's the perfect blend of ketchup and catsup!

You're <kanji>lack</kanji>ing something in your fridge. You look around, trying to find the <reading>ketsu</reading>p (けつ) you lack. You can't find it, because you lack it.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine having to use regular, ordinary ketchup, or just old, boring catsup on your burger. Or even worse, an actual tomato. BLEH!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Your <radical>clan</radical> is where you get your name. But not your given name, your <kanji>family name</kanji>. That's why people have names that mean "in a rice paddy" and "near the ferry crossing." The location of your clan determined your <kanji>surname</kanji>! Hope your ancestors didn't live on "Poo Lake" or something.
kanji.meaningHint: Think about your own surname in your language. Where did it come from? Were you a clan of village dwellers? Maybe you made shoes! You should look it up and find out!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Don't worry, I'll tell you where your <kanji>family name</kanji> came from. Your family used to herd <reading>shee</reading>p (し). You read that right, your family was of the sheep clan because you took care of sheep all day.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine your ancestors, herding sheep. Thanks to them your name means "sheep people." Thanks, great-great-great-great-great-grandpappy.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A giant <radical>cross</radical> with a <radical>mouth</radical> stands above you. "I am <kanji>reason</kanji>!" it says to you. It is the Cross of Reason.
kanji.meaningHint: Because it's a cross with a mouth, it thinks that it is reason in all the chaos.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>reason</kanji> that this Cross of Reason exists is to combat the <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう) of the world, who just bring chaos into everything.
kanji.readingHint: "Those youths just do things for no reason! That's why I, the Cross of Reason, am here! I will knock some reason into those youths."

kanji.meaningMnemonic: This <radical>tree</radical> has an <radical>umbrella</radical>, which it's holding over its head. Strange, because trees normally like water… Turns out, this tree wasn't getting showered in water, but in dollar <kanji>bill</kanji>s instead.
kanji.meaningHint: The sick part is that all those bills were once this tree's friends. Picture the tree sobbing uncontrollably, as pieces of its former friends fall everywhere around it. No wonder it needs that umbrella.
kanji.readingMnemonic: And the person who gave the tree an umbrella to protect it from all those <kanji>bills</kanji>? <reading>Satsu</reading>ki (さつ), a little girl famous for… handing out umbrellas, I guess. Makes sense that Satsuki would take care of these bills then.
kanji.readingHint: Try to remember this little girl named Satsuki, since she'll come up whenever the reading for a kanji is さつ (there's a good handful of them). Picture her in your mind, with details like her hair and clothes. Maybe even holding an umbrella or standing by a tree? You should also know she's kind of a bookworm, I guess, in terms of personality. If you can imagine her clearly now, it'll be easy to remember さつ kanji later on.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>mouth</radical> <radical>clan</radical> are a group of <kanji>people</kanji>. They are the <kanji>people</kanji> of a <kanji>nation</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: The mouth clan are distinct peoples. They do, of course, use their mouths.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The mouth clan <kanji>peoples</kanji> are a <kanji>nation</kanji> of <kanji>people</kanji> who use their mouths to say <reading>mean</reading> (みん) things to other peoples.
kanji.readingHint: That's why they're the mouth clan. This nation of people are known for mouthing off and saying mean things. Imagine them, as a nation, saying mean things to you. How awful! All being from the same place, they're all into it too. In a way, they're not the mouth clan, they're the mean clan.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: While riding your <radical>scooter</radical>, you take your <radical>sword</radical> and cut out an <kanji>area</kanji> on the ground.  You carefully cut all the <kanji>side</kanji>s as you go. This area's all yours now!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine riding your scooter around in a really large area, pressing your sword into the ground as you do. Once you've finished carving out the sides of the entire area, you claim to everyone around that this is YOUR area, and they aren't allowed in.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you look down at your <kanji>area</kanji> with its sword-carved <kanji>side</kanji>s, you suddenly realize there is a <reading>hen</reading> (へん) pecking at the ground in there. "Um, excuse me, hen, I believe I said this is MY area?!" You try to kick it out, but it hops over your leg.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine doing everything you can to get this hen out of your area, but it manages to dodge and outwit you at every turn. You even slash at it with your sword and try to run it over with your scooter, but the hen can't be stopped. This is the hen's area now. You have been defeated.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: When you take your <radical>leader</radical>'s <radical>measurement</radical>s, you realize they're too short, so you <kanji>attach</kanji> things to them to make the measurements more impressive. Attach some heels to the shoes, then attach another head on top of theirs. There — perfect measurements thanks to these attachments.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine guiding your leader's dainty feet into the heeled shoes, then attaching the weird head replica. Now picture yourself trying to keep a straight face as you tell them they totally look tall enough.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You have to remember the kun'yomi reading of this kanji, and the part you need to remember is つ. So, think of how you would <kanji>attach</kanji> something to something else. What would you need? You'd need <reading>two</reading> (つ) things to put together!
kanji.readingHint: Just focus on how attaching requires two things to remember this reading.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>lion</radical> drops a <radical>drop</radical> of saliva onto this <radical>person</radical> <kanji>from</kanji> above. The person is in a much worse place <kanji>compared with</kanji> where they were before, <kanji>since</kanji> they only just recently fell into this pit.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the person, the lion is leaning over them, the drop of spit dangling from their mouth. "I-I want to go back where I came from," the person gasps, shaking.
kanji.readingMnemonic: <kanji>From</kanji> above there is a loud caw, and a giant <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) swoops down, forcing the lion to back off. The eagle grabs the person with its talons, bringing him into the air! But now he's... in the air being carried by a giant eagle, <kanji>compared with</kanji> where he was before, is this really better?!
kanji.readingHint: The eagle came from the sky and technically rescued him, but compared to where he was before, it may not be a better situation. I think this person is going to be eaten either way.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: That <radical>slide</radical> is your <radical>husband</radical>'s only <kanji>fault</kanji>. He loves that slide, more than you, and it's the only thing you don't like about him.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine looking out the window of your house and watching your husband slide down his slide over and over. He's not even good at it, he falls off the side halfway down most of the time. You want to complain, but he's pretty decent otherwise. This is his only fault.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You try to come up with another <kanji>fault</kanji> of his so you can complain, when you see a tiny <reading>shih tzu</reading> (しつ) trotting by. Oh no! Before you can call out, your husband has fallen off the slide and crushed the poor thing. You hear a sharp yelp and then nothing.
kanji.readingHint: You run outside and yell, "AHA! It's your fault that shih tzu died! You and that stupid slide!"

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Your heart has a slide running through it because you want to be certain that the blood is flowing in and out of it smoothly. Given how important this is, you want to be absolutely certain.
kanji.meaningHint: Implanting a slide into your heart is certain to improve your cardiovascular health.
kanji.readingMnemonic: To be <kanji>certain</kanji> that the heart-slide is working, the doctor who put it there <reading>hits</reading> (ひつ) you in the chest a few times as a test.
kanji.readingHint: Feel the impact as the doctor hits you again and again. You're not certain that this is safe, but you do feel certain you've got a terrible doctor.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You're flying in a <radical>jet</radical>. Even though it's one of the fastest things on earth, your child is sitting in the back asking, "Are we there yet? Are we there yet?" You have to keep responding. "<kanji>Not yet</kanji>! Not yet! NOT YET!"
kanji.meaningHint: Feel the irritation of this. How irritating is this kid going to be the whole flight over? The jet is going as fast as it can!
kanji.readingMnemonic: What a selfish kid, right? Well, all he thinks about is "<reading>Me</reading> (み) me me me me me me me me me me." Hate kids like that.
kanji.readingHint: Go ahead and pretend to listen to the kid asking if we're there yet. Then in your mind go "me me me me me me me" quietly.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: This kanji uses a modified <radical>jet</radical> radical. The front area of the wing is wider than the middle area of the wing. This may seem counterintuitive, but by doing this they can fit so much more jet fuel. The jet zooms off and keeps going for a long, long time, until it reaches the <kanji>end</kanji> of the earth.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the end of the earth being like how they imagined it pre-Columbus era. Just a big drop going off into space, giant waterfalls plummeting down. Your crazy jet has made it to the very end! Congratulations!
kanji.readingMnemonic: When you get to the <kanji>end</kanji> of the world, you land your jet and put out a few <reading>mats</reading> (まつ) to sit on so you can view the sights.
kanji.readingHint: It's surprisingly dirty down here, because all the water takes the garbage this way. That's why you sit on these mats you brought.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Next to the <radical>tree</radical>, a <radical>lid</radical> is put on your <radical>father</radical>. "Hello child," he says. "This is your new <kanji>school</kanji>."
kanji.meaningHint: He goes on to explain that he changed your school to here because there is a tree to block the satellite's view. Also, he wears a tin foil lid on his head so they can't track him. The regular school was no good because "they were watching." So now you have this new school, taught under a tree by your father who's wearing a lid on his head.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your new <kanji>school</kanji> has other students too. They are all <reading>こう</reading>いちs, though.
kanji.readingHint: On your first day of school, imagine walking under the tree and seeing all your classmates. They're all こういち–similar to each other, but with some variation. Your father explains these こういちs escaped from a government research facility, and they come to this school to receive a better education.  "These poor こういちs need a school that will teach them more than just kanji and Japanese vocabulary."

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leaf</radical> shaped like an <radical>eye</radical> only grows in <radical>winter</radical>. Every other leaf, however, will do the opposite, which is to grow in the <kanji>summer</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Just think of the eye leaf as weird (it is weird, after all). It grows in the winter. Now, think of any normal leaves. They do the exact opposite, which is to grow in the summer.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Now it's summertime! What do you do during the <kanji>summer</kanji>? You just sit around with your favorite string tying <reading>knots</reading> (なつ) in it over and over again.
kanji.readingHint: Think about summer. Now think about yourself tying knots. Now think about summer again. Now think about tying knots again. Now think about your mother getting upset at you because all you do is tie knots all summer long. Go play video games like a normal kid!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have two <radical>bow</radical>s but they're both covered in <radical>ice</radical>. This has made them very <kanji>weak</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Just look at these weak, iced-over bows. If you tried to draw back their strings they'd snap into a million pieces.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You take the bows out to your car, which is stuck in a bunch of ice and snow, and try to use them as a kind of <kanji>weak</kanji> <reading>jack</reading> (じゃく). You know, to get your car unstuck. Unfortunately, your bows are too weak and brittle to use as jacks, and they just snap in half.
kanji.readingHint: Now you're stuck with two weak broken bows and no jack. Ice is the worst.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
The <radical>sun</radical> is used in a <radical>temple</radical> to tell <kanji>time</kanji>. They don't have clocks or cell phones, they have sun dials and good old fashioned "looking up and seeing where the sun is right now."

This also can mean <kanji>o' clock</kanji>, as in "five o'clock" It's used when measuring what time it is in Japanese.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine being in a temple and realizing you don't know what time it is. Never fear! Look on up at the sun. Ah, yes. Blinding noon.
kanji.readingMnemonic: <kanji>Time</kanji> in a temple makes you think of <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ). Specifically, Jesus being able to perform time travel magic. He winks at you, goes back to the dinosaur ages, where he wrestles a T-rex. Then, he goes to WWII era and punches Hitler in the mouth.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine him going to all kinds of different times and also make sure you're specifically imagining Jesus doing all these things. Put these two together and you'll remember the reading in no time. (Haha, get it?)

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>thread</radical> that ties you to your <radical>clan</radical> is <kanji>paper</kanji>. Your papers, that is.
kanji.meaningHint: The paper itself was also made by your clan using thread woven really tightly together.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You need this specific <kanji>paper</kanji> to prove that you aren't a <reading>Commi</reading> (かみ), aka a Communist. Or that you are. It really depends on where you want to go and what decade this is.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine a big guard coming up to you and asking to see your papers so they can see what clan you belong to. Well you're from the Commi clan, so you really hope this guard is okay with that.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: What you <radical>say</radical> to <radical>oneself</radical> (yourself), you decide to <kanji>write down</kanji>. Whether this is in the form of a journal, diary, or blog, you feel the need to <kanji>record</kanji> these important thoughts in some way.
kanji.meaningHint:
Just imagine writing in a diary and saying everything to write aloud to yourself in your head. 

"Dear me, today I learned a lot of new kanji on WaniKani. It was the best. I love the crabigator sooooo much. Love, me."
kanji.readingMnemonic: You need to protect what you <kanji>write down</kanji> and <kanji>record</kanji> for yourself with a <reading>key</reading> (き). These are your special thoughts and feelings, you don't want anyone else to see! Lock them away with a key!
kanji.readingHint: Picture the key you use to keep what you write down a secret. What does it look like? How does it feel in your hands?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>scooter</radical> with your <radical>mama</radical> carrying a <radical>task</radical> she needs to get done. You see her <kanji>pass through</kanji>, hurrying by to get that task done.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine your mama passing through your house on a scooter, not stopping because she needs to get her task done urgently.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you watch your mama <kanji>pass through</kanji> the house, she yells, "YOU HAVE TO DO THIS TASK <reading>TOO</reading> (つう)!" Too?! Oh no, now you have to do it too. Hurry up!
kanji.readingHint: Why do you have to do the task too? Because there are two tasks, so the two of you have to do them.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>lid</radical> on your <radical>mouth</radical> and <radical>mustache</radical>, covering up all your talking holes. This is because you kept saying how <kanji>tall</kanji> and <kanji>expensive</kanji> you are.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine yourself saying how tall and expensive you are to everyone in the room. Then they use a lid to cover your mouth so you can't talk to anyone anymore. But, then your mustache starts talking, saying the same thing. That's why this lid covers both your mustache and your mouth. Now you can't say that you are tall or expensive.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
"I am <kanji>tall</kanji>er and more <kanji>expensive</kanji> than you." 

You're saying this because there are some <reading>こう</reading>いちs in the room, and you want to make them feel inferior (you're a こういち hater). You keep comparing your height to the こういちs in the room, and you keep checking price tags. Then you tell them you're taller and more expensive than they are.
kanji.readingHint: The こういちs finally get tired of your shenanigans, and lid up your mouth and mustache so you can't say that you're tall or expensive.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You keep your <radical>bow</radical> <radical>private</radical> because it's made of <radical>insect</radical>s, meaning it's extremely <kanji>strong</kanji>. Insect bodies are really durable, so they make for super strong bows. That's why you have to keep this one private — it's simply too strong to let others get ahold of.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine holding this bow. Feel how strong it is as you draw the string. Now look closely at the insect bodies it's made of. Thanks for your help, little guys.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You had this <kanji>strong</kanji> bow made especially for you in <reading>きょう</reading>と. きょうと is famous for their strong bows, so if you ever want another, you know where to go.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine all the people who live in きょうと, using their strong arms to make strong bows out of strong insect carapaces. Could きょうと be Japan's strongest city?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>teacher</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> is happiest because they get to <kanji>teach</kanji>! The kids can't go out and play because it's too cold. They all have to come in and stay warm as the teacher teaches!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a teacher excitedly teaching, bundled up in the cold. Snow falling outside. Grumpy children being taught inside.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Teachers can teach the most about Japan in winter by going to <reading>きょう</reading>と. きょうと is where all the old temples and history of Japan is centered. And it's really gorgeous when it snows.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the teaching teacher teaching you about Japan in きょうと in winter. You've always wanted to go to きょうと!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>king</radical>'s <radical>village</radical> is the <kanji>reason</kanji> he's king. Without the village there would be no reason to have a king in the first place.
kanji.meaningHint: If a king has no one to rule then he has no reason to exist.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You can't have <kanji>reason</kanji> without <reading>re</reading> (り).
kanji.readingHint: Just like you can't have a king without a village, you can't have reason without re.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Sew <radical>thread</radical> through your <radical>top hat</radical> and to the top hats of other people you know and you'll turn into a <kanji>group</kanji> of top hat wearing people. You're all connected by the thread now, so everyone will assume you're a group, even if that's all you guys have going for yourselves.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a group of people threaded together by their top hats. Don't you want to be part of a cool group like that? Your own top hat team.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Everyone in this <kanji>group</kanji> loves <reading>cumi</reading>n (くみ). You know, the spice or seed. The group take off their top hats and fill them with cumin. You're officially a group for lovers of cumin.
kanji.readingHint: What do you do in the cumin group? You smell the cumin. Cook with it. Taste it. This group lives and breathes cumin!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Your <radical>boat</radical> has <radical>fins</radical> and a <radical>mouth</radical>! It's still a <kanji>boat</kanji> though.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture this boat. It's still a boat, but there is a big mouth on the front and it has fins that it paddles forward with.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>boat</kanji> belongs to the <reading>cen</reading>taurs (せん). That's probably why you've never seen a boat like it before.
kanji.readingHint: Picture this mouth and boat with a bunch of centaurs riding in it. Centaurs have a lot more parts than humans, so it makes sense that their boats have more parts (animal ones) too.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Use a <radical>scooter</radical> to travel the <radical>circumference</radical> of the world and it will take you a full <kanji>week</kanji>. Seven whole days!
kanji.meaningHint: A week in earth time is also known as a "full scoot" in scooter lingo. ;)
kanji.readingMnemonic: If you want to scoot for a <kanji>week</kanji>, you'll need <reading>shoe</reading>s (しゅう). Good shoes too, not sandals or high heels or boots. Solid, high quality shoes, so you don't fall off the scooter and hurt yourself.
kanji.readingHint: You can't ride a scooter for a week barefoot, are you nuts?! Get some shoes!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: When <radical>rain</radical> falls on <radical>Wolverine</radical>, it turns to <kanji>snow</kanji>. He's so emotionally distant and cold that the rain freezes into snow as soon as it gets near him.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine Wolverine in the pouring rain, creating a little halo of snow around him wherever he goes. It's strangely beautiful. That is one cold, traumatized dude…
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're concerned for Wolverine's mental health. Him being so emotionally cold that he turns rain to <kanji>snow</kanji> means <reading>you kee</reading>p (ゆき) asking if he's okay. But that only makes him want to be more distant.
kanji.readingHint: Sheesh, emotionally distant people are complicated. The more you keep trying to help them, the more they reject you. Wolverine could do with a nice holiday to melt all that snow away.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>fish</radical> and the kanji <kanji>fish</kanji> are exactly the same!
kanji.meaningHint: Nothing fishy about that, right?
kanji.readingMnemonic: You catch a <kanji>fish</kanji>. As you pull it out of the water, it starts yelling and pointing: "<reading>GO</reading>!" (ぎょ). "GO GYO GYO GYO!" There's a huge cruise ship coming right towards your little fishing boat. No wonder the fish was yelling GO at you.
kanji.readingHint: Have him continue to scream "GO GYO GYO GYO!" as you try to get your engine started and attempt to flee your impending doom. The fish helps too, because he's pretty worried as well.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>bird</radical> radical and the <kanji>bird</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: As long as you know the radical bird you know the kanji bird.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Think of a run-of-the-mill <kanji>bird</kanji>, whatever comes to mind for you first is fine. Then, your lovely bird swells. The shape of a face, then a hand, start stretching the bird apart until it explodes outward. Covered in blood and feathers is Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう).
kanji.readingHint: After bursting out of this bird, she turns her head sharply in your direction. "I don't just own the streets, I own the birds too. I'm inside every bird, and I, Mrs. Chou, can burst out at any time."

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>yellow</radical> and the kanji <kanji>yellow</kanji> are exactly the same!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're in a room, surrounded completely by <kanji>yellow</kanji>. You can't get out. Somewhere in the room is a yellow <reading>key</reading> (き) but you can't find it, because everything looks the same. You crawl around trying to find this tiny thing so that you can escape.
kanji.readingHint: The walls are coming in closer, too. Make sure you feel a bit of peril as you look for this key. The walls have a slight opening at the bottom too, so if you don't find it before the wall goes over it, the key will be lost forever, and you'll be smushed!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>black</radical> and the kanji <kanji>black</kanji> are exactly the same.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're in a completely <kanji>black</kanji> room. There's no way out, and you can't see. The room starts to fill with liquid. It gets in your mouth. You taste it. It's <reading>Coke</reading> (こく)! Mm, tasty Coke.
kanji.readingHint: You need to drink all this Coke, otherwise you're going to drown. Drink this Coke and keep tasting its cold sweetness as you drink it all to survive.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
You look at a <radical>table</radical> and notice it is being used as a <radical>slide</radical> by <radical>insect</radical>s to launch themselves into the <kanji>wind</kanji>.

This kanji can also mean <kanji>style</kanji>. To remember this, consider how styles can change quickly, just like the <kanji>wind</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a table tilted on its side with some of its legs longer than others, a perfect slide for insects! Imagine all the different insects jumping into the wind each in their own particular style.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You wonder what's pushing these insects to jump into the <kanji>wind</kanji> in such a manner, and you realize that it's because they've had way too much <reading>foo</reading>d (ふう).
kanji.readingHint: The insects ate all the food that was left on the table, and now they can't just fly away into the wind like they normally do. Instead, they have to try this new style by using the table as a slide to help them take off into the wind.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> in the <radical>center</radical> of the sky gives off its light, which <kanji>reflect</kanji>s off of everything around it.
kanji.meaningHint: Look around you, everything you see is reflecting the light of the sun. Unless it's night time, then the tiny sun in the center of your lightbulb is creating the light that reflects there.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>reflect</kanji>ed light is important for <reading>a</reading>corns (えい), in particular. Without light reflecting off everything, the sun's light would never make it down to the ground where they've fallen. They would never grow into trees. And we'd all suffocate.
kanji.readingHint: Picture the light of the sun reflecting off a single acorn on the forest floor. So much symbolism!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>elephant</radical> radical and the <kanji>elephant</kanji> kanji are the same. But! This kanji has another meaning: <kanji>phenomenon</kanji>. If you were the first person to see an elephant, you'd call it that too.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the first Japanese person to see an elephant. He stops dead in his tracks, points and screams out, "What a phenomenon!"
kanji.readingMnemonic:
<kanji>Elephant</kanji>s are great and all, except that when they die they turn into elephant <reading>zo</reading>mbies (ぞう). But you never see these zombies because the <reading>shou</reading>gun (しょう) has a special project in place that destroys all elephant bodies when they die.

Hint: The readings and meanings for this kanji match up really nicely. ぞう is always for elephant and しょう is always for phenomenon. Remember it like this, the elephant is the zombie and the shougun keeps everyone from finding out about this phenomenon.
kanji.readingHint: Picture the shougun standing over a pit of zombie elephants. None of these are getting out on his watch, letting people believe in such crazy phenomenons.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Under the <radical>canopy</radical>, you use a <radical>tree</radical> for your <kanji>floor</kanji>. It also becomes your <kanji>bed</kanji>, because hey, what is a floor but the original bed?
kanji.meaningHint: You lay it down, cut it into slats, and voila! A floor! And a bed!
kanji.readingMnemonic: It's great having a <kanji>floor</kanji> or <kanji>bed</kanji>, but whenever you use it you say <reading>yucka</reading> (ゆか) because it just gets so dirty. That's the one flaw of using a floor as a bed. In fact, it's the dirtiest floor you've ever seen, because it's covered in <reading>yucca</reading> (ゆか) leaves. You're sleeping on a yucca floor. Ew!
kanji.readingHint: You can imagine how comfortable it is to sleep on a floor of yucca leaves, but at the same time how horrible the smell must be when they start to rot.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う (in this case る) sound, you know this word is a verb. One of the kanji meanings is <kanji>divide</kanji>, which makes this <vocabulary>to divide something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to separate something</vocabulary>. Depending on the context, it can also mean <vocabulary>to share</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to classify</vocabulary>.

Be careful not to confuse this with 分かる, a similar word with a different meaning. Think of it this way: You "separate" what you care (ける) about from everything else. You want to separate those special things you care about from all the other things you don't care about.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already know this reading from 分かる, but here’s a mnemonic in case you forgot:

Whenever you need <vocabulary>to divide something</vocabulary>, you can’t help screaming "<reading>WAAAAAAAAAHHHH</reading>" (わ). You hate having to divide things, or people, so you always end up screaming "WAAAAAAAAAHHHH" in agony.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word starts with an お to make it more polite. Then it has the kanji <kanji>兄</kanji> which you already know. Lastly, it has さん which is an honorific to elevate people and be polite. This is basically the formal way of saying <vocabulary>older brother</vocabulary> (versus plain old 兄). It can also be used to refer to a <vocabulary>guy</vocabulary> that you don't know who has a youthful appearance.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The reading for this one is pretty tricky, and I'd consider it an exception. To remember it, you have to learn the 兄 part, and everything else will fall into place. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your (kind) <vocabulary>older brother</vocabulary> pushes you down on the ground. You stand up and look at your <reading>knee</reading> (にい), which is all bloody. "Why'd you do that to my knee!?" you ask. "You're supposed to be a nice older brother, that's why I call you お兄さん!"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>substitute</kanji>, and the verb 代わる means <vocabulary>to substitute for</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to take over for</vocabulary>. Use it when one player substitutes for another in sports, for example, or when someone takes over for you at work. 

代わる is usually intransitive, but sometimes it can be transitive and take a direct object. Kind of like "to take over" in English — someone can take over your shift (transitive), or just take over for you (intransitive).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember the か part:

You need something <vocabulary>to substitute for</vocabulary> your <reading>car</reading> (か). It's getting repaired, so you can't use it now. I guess you can substitute your bike for your car?

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You learned this reading with 考える, just cut off the る!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: 考える means "to think," right? Well, the <kanji>way</kanji> you think is your <vocabulary>way of thinking</vocabulary>. In other words, it's your <vocabulary>thought process</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This word uses kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You learned the かんが reading with 考える, but かた wasn't the main reading you learned for 方, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

Your <vocabulary>way of thinking</vocabulary> is like a <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた). You just launch ideas at the wall and see what sticks. Sure it's a bit inexact, but it's the best <vocabulary>thought process</vocabulary> for you. The catapult way of thinking just suits you!

What <vocabulary>shape</vocabulary> do you <reading>cut a chee</reading>se (かたち) into? Stars, triangles, little cubes, hearts! Anything but the boring slices other people do. You're like a mozzarella Michelangelo, the way you cut a cheese into those beautifully sculpted <vocabulary>form</vocabulary>s.

Because only men got the respect back in the day, we're calling this vocab word <vocabulary>mister</vocabulary>. You can call me Mr. Koichi if you'd like, too.

A <kanji>reason</kanji> <kanji>reason</kanji> is a <vocabulary>reason</vocabulary>! How could it not be? Do you have a reason why it shouldn't be? I thought not.

This word means "reason" as in the reason you're studying Japanese, or the reason you're late. That's why it can also mean similar words like <vocabulary>motive</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>excuse</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

You'll also see this pronounced ふだ, but that's when it's a standalone word or part of a compound, rather than a suffix. So if you answer with that reading, you'll be prompted to enter the suffix reading instead.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know what 千円 is (1000 yen). So if you add a <kanji>bill</kanji> to that you get a <vocabulary>thousand yen bill</vocabulary>. That's just the little rectangular piece of money that is worth 1000 yen.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for the kanji portion is just what you've already learned with the kanji 辺 so this shouldn't be a difficult one to read for you.

Start <kanji>from</kanji> something and then go <kanji>above</kanji> it. Now you have "<vocabulary>no less than</vocabulary> ___," or, in other words, "___ <vocabulary>or more</vocabulary>"! 

When used with numbers, 以上 always includes the number itself, like 十人以上 (10 or more people). In non-numerical contexts, it can mean "more than" in a looser sense, like これ以上もてない (I can't carry more than this).

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The kanji portion means <kanji>fault</kanji>, so you would think the verb version is "to fault." It's a little different, though. Think of it this way, if you "fault" something, you're messing up. What's a great way to mess up? By losing something. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to lose</vocabulary>. 

Pretend like you are supposed to hold on to someone's wedding ring. You make the biggest fault of all. You lose it. Ouch.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

So how did you lose the wedding ring anyway? Well... it was eaten by a cow. The <reading>牛 now</reading> (うし + なう) has to have it surgically removed. What a mess!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
When you do something that's your <kanji>fault</kanji> and then you say "<kanji>thanks</kanji>" after you do it, that's super-duper <vocabulary>rude</vocabulary>, wouldn't you say? Imagine doing something like this and then thinking to yourself after... wow, I was really rude.

This is also often used to mean <vocabulary>excuse me</vocabulary>, typically followed by ですが or します. Occasionally, it’s also used just on its own, usually when the speaker holds a higher or equal status to the person being spoken to. This particular usage is more prevalent among older generations and is commonly associated with masculine speech.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word looks like a verb but it's not (sorry!). It's an adverb. The kanji itself means <kanji>certain</kanji> and the vocab version means all sorts of variations on that: <vocabulary>surely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>certainly</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>without exception</vocabulary> to name a few.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Ra, the Egyptian god asks you: "Can you do it? Are you <vocabulary>certain</vocabulary> you can build the pyramids?" 

"Yes I <reading>can ra</reading> (かなら). Yes I can," you reply.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Your future consists of <kanji>certain</kanji> <kanji>death</kanji>. How would you feel in this situation? Probably very <vocabulary>frantic</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>desperate</vocabulary>. 

Another translation for this word is simply <vocabulary>certain death</vocabulary>, though I'd rather you learn one of the first two before this one if you can.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are the on'yomi readings, though 必 (ひつ) gets shortened to ひっ. In your <vocabulary>desperate</vocabulary> situation just imagine that you're trying to get out of it, and to do so you move the つ only to find a smaller っ blocking your way. It is certain death.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
What has <kanji>not yet</kanji> <kanji>come</kanji>? The <vocabulary>future</vocabulary>.

未来 is usually used to talk about the distant future, and it implies that the future can’t be foreseen. So you can use it to speculate about what might lie ahead, but you probably wouldn’t use it to discuss more concrete plans, goals or predictions.

You've reached <vocabulary>the end</vocabulary> of the universe. Nothing is there. You step out, and you're surprised because you get greeted by an old Canadian man. <reading>Sue, eh?</reading>(すえ) he asks you, over and over. The poor man is looking for his wife Sue, and he's searched to the end of the universe. That's true love. As he walks off into the distance, you hear him calling out, "Sue, eh? Sue, eh? Sue, eh?"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>tall</kanji> <kanji>school</kanji> is for when your kids get about as tall as they're going to get. That's <vocabulary>high school</vocabulary>, when most people stop growing taller.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

You <kanji>correct</kanji> the <kanji>moon</kanji> because it's a <vocabulary>New Year</vocabulary>. It's the beginning of a fresh year, so you gotta have the moon in the correct position.

正月 usually refers to the first few days of a new year, and it's one of the biggest holidays in Japan. Originally, it meant the entire first month of the new year, so you still might see it used that way in some contexts — especially historical ones.

Note: Since 正月 used to refer to the entire first month of the new year, it uses the がつ reading of 月 — the reading used for specific month names.

仕組み refers to the concept of a "mechanism" or "system." It includes the underlying structure, organization, or framework that governs how something works or operates, highlighting its logic, order, and other often unseen things.

西日 describes the sun when it's in the western part of the sky. It generally refers to the afternoon sun, but it can also mean the <vocabulary>setting sun</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>evening sun</vocabulary>. Basically, you can use it for sun or sunlight from mid-afternoon until sunset!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bright</kanji>, but the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to dawn</vocabulary>. It gets bright each morning when a new day dawns, so the connection kinda makes sense, right?

While 明ける is commonly used with 夜 to talk about the dawn breaking, it's also often used to talk about other time-related transitions. Because of this, it can mean <vocabulary>to end</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> depending on the situation, as in 冬休みが明ける (winter vacation ends) or 年が明ける (the new year begins). Think of it like a new phase in your life is "dawning."
